main_result: VERIFIED from abstract/body snippets (Wiley page https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2664.12519; ResearchGate 281406494; academia.edu copies): The paper tested whether long-term abundance time series of 55 taxa (126 data sets) across multiple trophic levels in marine and freshwater ecosystems showed (i) significant nonlinear change in abundance ("turning points") and (ii) significant increases in variance and lag-1 autocorrelation ("early warning indicators", EWIs), and quantified true positives (EWI with an associated turning point), false negatives (turning point without associated EWI) and false positives (EWI without turning point). Results: at the time-series level, series containing true positives were uncommon (8% for variance; 6% for autocorrelation), and all but one time series also contained false classifications; at the event/"case" level, true positives were 9% (16 of 170) of cases for variance and 13% (19 of 152) for autocorrelation; false positives were more prevalent than false negatives (53% vs 38% for variance; 47% vs 40% for autocorrelation); false results occurred in every decade and across all trophic levels and ecosystems; coherence between the two indicators was low, with 43% of time series categorized differently by variance vs autocorrelation. Conclusion (abstract): variance and autocorrelation "consistently fail to predict nonlinear change"; the authors recommend multivariate suites of indicators incorporating anthropogenic drivers and process-based understanding. Note: the exact location (abstract vs Results) of the 9%/13% "cases" figures vs the 8%/6% series-level figures could not be resolved from snippets; both sets of numbers appeared in multiple independent snippets. Confidence in these numbers: high (repeated verbatim across Wiley, ResearchGate/academia and citing-paper snippets).
what_it_does_NOT_do_relative_to_our_task: Relative to our preregistered design, Burthe et al. (2016), as far as visible in search snippets, does NOT: (1) make sequential, fixed-horizon (1-5 y) predictions from forecast origins using only data available at each origin - it is a retrospective "temporal coherence" analysis in which a GAM is fitted to the whole standardized series and turning points and indicator state-changes are identified post hoc (VERIFIED method description; "not time-indexed" is our INFERENCE from that description); (2) use any out-of-sample or hindcast validation (no snippet mentions holdout, cross-validation or hindcasting); (3) compare EWIs against any state/trend or forecasting baseline - the only comparison is between the two EWIs (variance vs autocorrelation coherence); (4) calibrate alarm thresholds or output probabilities; (5) impose a false-alarm budget or match false-positive rates between competing predictors - false positives are counted but not budgeted; (6) target population collapse: the outcome is any "significant turning point" in a GAM smooth (state change of the first derivative among stationary/positive/negative), described by O'Brien et al. 2023 as "generic indicators of nonlinear change, which may have included both catastrophic and non-catastrophic transitions" (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43744-8; bioRxiv version), and by Litzow et al. 2016 as breakpoint analysis without a test for nonlinearity/critical transition (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecs2.1614); it is not "first collapse" and direction (decline vs increase) is not distinguished in any snippet we saw; (7) use a 1-5 y horizon - it uses a 10-year association window chosen "in the absence of a priori information on the time-scale over which EWIs would precede abundance change"; (8) treat right-censoring/complete follow-up - handling of EWI increases near series ends (where a turning point could not yet be observed) is not visible in search results; (9) span realms - all six systems are UK aquatic (two lakes, Cumbrian lakes, North Sea CPR, Isle of May seabirds); no fisheries stock assessments (RAM), GPDD, Living Planet, BioTIME or terrestrial data; (10) use a combined EWS score or capacity-matched learners - variance and autocorrelation are assessed separately with a rolling window of 25% of the data; (11) group results by biological system with formal system-level inference (results are described as false results "in every decade and across all trophic levels and ecosystems", but a formal grouped test is not visible).
threat_reasoning: Burthe et al. 2016 is the most prominent multi-series empirical EWS test with an explicit true-positive/false-negative/false-positive tally, so it must be cited prominently and it settles one thing we must NOT claim: prior work did not ignore false positives or non-transitioning periods - Burthe et al. counted false positives explicitly and found them more prevalent than false negatives (53% vs 38% variance; 47% vs 40% autocorrelation) (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2664.12519). However, every element of our novelty combination is absent from their design as far as the search snippets show: it is retrospective (whole-series GAM turning-point detection and post hoc coherence within a 10-year window), has no forecast origins, no out-of-sample validation, no state/trend or forecasting baseline, no calibration, no matched false-alarm burden, no explicit censoring rule, an outcome that is generic nonlinear change rather than collapse, and coverage limited to six UK aquatic systems (126 series, 55 taxa). It also analyses variance and autocorrelation separately rather than as a prespecified composite score, and at annual resolution after averaging sub-annual plankton data. Our manuscript can position itself as moving from Burthe's retrospective coherence framing (does an indicator change co-occur with a turning point within 10 years?) to a prequential, baseline-controlled, calibrated detection framing for first collapses across realms. The main residual risk is framing, not overlap: reviewers may treat our study as a re-test of a settled negative and ask what the baseline comparison adds; the answer is that Burthe never asked whether EWIs add detection beyond what current state and trend already give at equal false-alarm cost. Note also that citing reviews (Dakos et al. 2024 ESD https://esd.copernicus.org/articles/15/1117/2024/; Arumugam et al. 2024 Ecology https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecy.4240; Rohde et al. 2022 https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eap.2685) summarize it as evidence that EWIs "fail" or have "low detectability prior to identified breakpoints" - consistent with our characterization.

VERIFIED steps (snippets from the Wiley full text via search results): (a) each abundance time series was first standardized by fitting a GAM (log link, intercept for overall mean abundance, a day-of-year term for the within-year relationship, and a thin-plate regression spline smooth of time), to allow non-normal error structure; analysis was at an inter-annual scale (26 series originally annual; the remaining plankton series - 15 monthly-average and 85 finer-than-monthly with uneven gaps - were converted to annual mean chlorophyll-a or counts); (b) turning points were identified from the first derivative of the fitted GAM smooth, classifying the trend into three states (stationary, positive, negative); the first-derivative approach was chosen "because of the requirement to classify the trend into the three states ... as the second derivative method cannot inform on periods of stationarity"; (c) lag-1 autocorrelation and variance were extracted over a rolling window corresponding to 25% of the data using the R package 'earlywarnings'; (d) "the extracted autocorrelation and variance series were subjected to the same routine as the abundance time series to determine when any significant changes in the state of the indicator had occurred"; a snippet states that only changes from a positive state to a stationary state and from a stationary to a positive state were considered ecologically informative (this appears to refer to the indicator series - i.e., an increase in the EWI - but the snippet is ambiguous); (e) a true positive was declared when the indicator change preceded a significant turning point within a 10-year period. Because the GAM smooth and its derivative are estimated from the entire series, turning-point timing and indicator state changes both use future information; there are no sequential forecast origins and no restriction to data available at each origin. No snippet mentions forecast origins, prospective evaluation, or lead-time distributions beyond the 10-year window. Sources: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2664.12519 (via search snippets); Litzow et al. 2016 characterize it as defining "nonlinear change as turning points in predicted values from generalized additive models (GAMs) fit to time series" (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecs2.1614).

design_false_alarms: VERIFIED: false positives were explicitly defined ("early warning indicators but no turning point") and counted alongside false negatives ("turning point but no associated early warning indicators") and true positives ("early warning indicators and associated turning point"), with association judged within a 10-year window; result: false positives more prevalent than false negatives (53% vs 38% for variance; 47% vs 40% for autocorrelation), and all but one time series contained at least one false classification (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2664.12519; also summarized in https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13298826/). This means non-transitioning periods within series are included in the denominators (event-level "cases": 170 for variance, 152 for autocorrelation; the differing denominators are consistent with cases = TP+FN+FP events per indicator - INFERENCE). NOT visible: whether whole series without any turning point were retained (implied yes, since FPs are counted per data set); whether a fixed false-alarm burden was imposed or matched across indicators (no); any exclusion or special handling of indicator increases in the final 10 years of a series (near series ends) - "not visible in search results"; any edge-effect treatment for the 25% rolling window - "not visible in search results".
design_horizon_and_censoring: VERIFIED: "Burthe et al. considered 10 years to be an appropriate period within which to assess the relationship between early warning indicators and turning points in the absence of a priori information on the time-scale over which EWIs would precede abundance change"; a true positive is an indicator change that preceded a significant turning point within a 10-year period (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2664.12519 via search snippets). So the horizon is a single 10-year association window, not fixed 1-5 y horizons, and no lead-time distribution was visible in snippets. Censoring: no snippet mentions right-censoring, follow-up completeness, or how indicator increases occurring within 10 years of the end of a series (where the outcome cannot yet be observed) were classified - "not visible in search results"; our INFERENCE (medium confidence) is that such events would have been counted as false positives, which is the exact issue our complete-follow-up rule addresses, but this is not confirmed.

(2016) adopted a flexible approach by considering turning points as generic indicators of nonlinear change, which may have included both catastrophic and non-catastrophic transitions" (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43744-8; https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.05.11.540304v1.full.pdf); Litzow et al. 2016 - "defined nonlinear change as turning points in predicted values from generalized additive models (GAMs) fit to time series" and cite it among studies using breakpoint analyses as evidence of shifts without rigorously testing for nonlinearity (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecs2.1614). Not collapse-specific, not first-event-specific, and not direction-specific as far as visible (which state transitions of the abundance smooth counted as turning points - e.g., positive-to-negative only vs any - is "not visible in search results"). A snippet stating that only positive-to-stationary and stationary-to-positive changes were "ecologically informative ... indicative of a change to a new state or an increase in EWI preceding change" most plausibly refers to the indicator series, but attribution is ambiguous.
data_and_sample: VERIFIED: 126 abundance data sets for 55 taxa, six aquatic study systems comprising shallow lake, deep lake and coastal marine ecosystems, all trophic levels from r-selected phytoplankton (primary producers) to K-selected apex predators (seabirds); one snippet (attribution uncertain, possibly Rohde et al. 2022 or the paper itself) says "four trophic levels". Systems/data visible in snippets: (1) North Sea Continuous Plankton Recorder (SAHFOS CPR) monthly phytoplankton and zooplankton from 55-58N, 3W-0E, chosen for proximity to the Isle of May; the ten most abundant diatom species and zooplankton species important in the diet of sandeels (Ammodytes marinus); data from David Johns at SAHFOS. (2) Isle of May NNR, Scotland: annual whole-island counts of breeding pairs for five seabird species (Atlantic puffin, common guillemot, razorbill, European shag, black-legged kittiwake). (3) Cumbrian lakes (Blelham Tarn, Esthwaite Water, Windermere north and south basins; Freshwater Biological Association/CEH monitoring): phytoplankton and crustacean zooplankton at weekly-to-fortnightly intervals (zooplankton at species level for Windermere north basin, aggregate counts for other lakes), chlorophyll-a, and fish catch data. (4) Loch Leven, Scotland: plankton at weekly-to-monthly intervals; autumn and winter waterfowl counts 1968-2006 (SNH/RSPB data; Kinross Estates access). Temporal resolution: analysis at inter-annual scale; 26 series originally annual; 15 monthly-average series and 85 finer-than-monthly series (all plankton) were converted to annual means (26+15+85 = 126). Rolling window for EWIs = 25% of the data. Funding: CEH Ecological Resilience project, NERC; JNCC support for Isle of May. main_result: VERIFIED (abstract, multiple sources: nature.com, PMC10692136, PubMed 38040724, NSF PAR, Bristol repository): Using multi-trophic planktonic data on multiple lakes worldwide, the authors classified lake dynamics and assessed the reliability of "classic and second generation" EWS methods to predict whole-ecosystem change. They "find few instances of critical transitions, with different trophic levels often expressing different forms of abrupt change"; "the ability to predict this change is highly processing dependent, with most indicators not performing better than chance, multivariate EWSs being weakly superior to univariate, and a recent machine learning model performing poorly." They conclude predictive ecology should move away from the concept of critical transitions and develop methods for predicting resilience loss not limited to bifurcation theory. VERIFIED details from search snippets of the full text: (i) critical transitions (breakpoint in plankton density coherent with a breakpoint in the environmental state space plus bimodality/hysteresis criteria) were identified only in Lake Kasumigaura zooplankton, Lake Kinneret phytoplankton, Lake Monona zooplankton and Lake Washington phytoplankton; other lakes had time-series breakpoints (e.g., Mendota and Windermere zooplankton) not matched in environmental state space, classified as "abrupt non-bifurcations" if bimodal (nature.com / par.nsf.gov snippets). (ii) ar1 was "the most reliable rolling window univariate EWS for critical transitions"; multivariate rolling-window indicators (meanAR, pcaSD, eigenMAF) were "particularly effective in transitioning time series but weak in non-transitioning data" (nature.com snippet). (iii) The EWSNet machine-learning model: unscaled EWSNet true-positive probability 0.93 (monthly) and 0.89 (yearly) but true-negative probability 0.19 and 0.05; scaled EWSNet the inverse (TP 0.13/0.07; TN 0.76/0.97) (published-version snippet via Bristol/NSF PDF; the bioRxiv-derived snippet gives 0.92/0.88, 0.2/0.06, 0.12/0.08, 0.77/0.97 -- slight version differences). (iv) "Strong methodological influences upon EWS ability exist regardless of computation method, specifically through the choice of time series pre-processing, resolution of time series, and aggregation of time series to genus vs trophic level" (PMC snippet). (v) Overall stated conclusion: generic EWS predictive ability is limited and some system-specific knowledge appears necessary; "with real world time series, there is no ideal data for EWSs due to their typically high variability and cyclical nature driving false positive warnings" (PMC snippet).
what_it_does_NOT_do_relative_to_our_task: Based on what was visible in search snippets (medium confidence; full Methods not read): (1) Outcome is ecosystem-level regime shift / critical transition in lake plankton (phytoplankton and zooplankton density), NOT first population collapse of monitored populations, and NOT cross-realm (only 9 freshwater lakes). (2) Evaluation is a retrospective per-series binary classification (did the indicator signal in a series known a posteriori to be critically transitioning vs not), summarized with Bayesian binomial models against a 50-50 chance reference; there is no sequential fixed-horizon forecasting from multiple time-indexed origins, no lead-time/horizon (1-5 yr) analysis, and no out-of-sample validation of alarm thresholds or of any fitted component (no "out-of-sample", "hindcast" or "forecast origin" language found). (3) No conventional state-and-trend forecasting comparator (current abundance vs reference, recent slope, state-space threshold-crossing forecast); the only comparator is chance and, in relative terms, other EWS families (univariate vs multivariate vs EWSNet). (4) No calibration of alarm probabilities and no explicit, matched false-alarm budget: thresholds are fixed conventions (expanding-window 2-sigma exceeded for >2 consecutive points; rolling-window positive Kendall tau, exact tau cut-off for this paper not visible) and true-positive and true-negative probabilities are reported separately rather than compared at equalized false-alarm rates. (5) No capacity-matched learners; the ML model (EWSNet) is a pretrained generic model applied as-is (scaled/unscaled). (6) Outcome labels come from threshold GAM breakpoints over the whole series, so there is no prospective follow-up, censoring handling or "complete follow-up" concept. (7) Sample is small in independent systems (9 lakes, 2 trophic levels; series aggregated to monthly and yearly, 9-30 yr after truncation) though genus-level series inflate the count of assessed series. (8) Classical univariate EWS were tested, but the authors' headline is about processing dependence and the rarity of true critical transitions rather than an incremental-value comparison against forecasting baselines.
threat_reasoning: This is the most relevant prior empirical benchmark for the lake-regime-shift challenge analysis and must be cited and positioned carefully, because it (a) explicitly assessed EWS in both transitioning and non-transitioning series and reported true-negative (i.e., false-alarm) probabilities, (b) tested classic univariate indicators (ar1, SD, skewness, kurtosis and combinations), multivariate indicators and an ML model, (c) used several of the same public lake datasets we may use (Loch Leven, Mendota, Monona, Washington, Windermere, Zurich), and (d) reached a negative conclusion ("most indicators not performing better than chance"). Our stated novelty is the COMBINATION of sequential fixed-horizon prediction + out-of-sample validation + matched state/trend baselines + calibration + explicit false-alarm budget + complete follow-up, for population-abundance collapse across realms; none of those design elements is visible in this paper (its comparator is 50-50 chance, its evaluation is retrospective per-series classification with fixed thresholds, and its outcome is ecosystem regime shift in lakes). Therefore the threat to the main claim is low; for the lake challenge analysis specifically the overlap in data and in "transitioning vs non-transitioning" framing is moderate, so the manuscript should state explicitly that O'Brien et al. did not ignore false positives (they reported TN probabilities) and that our contribution there is the prequential, baseline-matched, calibrated design rather than the mere inclusion of non-transitioning series.

design_baseline: No state-and-trend forecasting baseline. VERIFIED: performance was summarised with "Bayesian binomial models ... to test the ability of each EWS computation method and individual indicators to correctly predict the transition fate (critically transitioning versus not)", with figures showing "the zero-slope -- i.e., 50-50 chance of correct prediction" as the reference and 1000 posterior samples (bioRxiv/nature.com snippets). Comparators are therefore chance and other EWS families (univariate vs multivariate; rolling vs expanding window; EWSNet scaled vs unscaled; monthly vs yearly; genus vs trophic aggregation; raw vs detrended). No comparison with current-abundance-relative-to-reference, recent-slope or state-space threshold-crossing forecasts is visible.
design_calibration: Not visible; apparently none. Alarm rules are fixed conventions: expanding-window indicators exceeding the 2-sigma threshold for more than two consecutive time points identified warnings (snippet); rolling-window warnings rely on a strong positive Kendall tau with time (the specific tau cut-off used in this paper is not visible in search results; the authors' EWSmethods vignette notes published cut-offs range 0.5-0.9 and that a permutation-based alternative exists). EWSNet outputs a class probability but no recalibration is mentioned; the "scaled vs unscaled" contrast refers to scaling of training/input data, not probability calibration. Results are reported as posterior probabilities of correct prediction from Bayesian binomial models, not as calibrated forecast probabilities or reliability diagrams.

Censoring is not applicable in their design: outcome labels (critical transition, abrupt non-bifurcation, non-transitioning) come from threshold GAM breakpoints and bimodality/hysteresis tests applied retrospectively to complete series, so there are no right-censored origins -- but equally no prospective follow-up concept. outcome_definition: VERIFIED (snippets): Regime shifts were detected with threshold generalised additive models (TGAMs) of (yearly) total plankton density against time and against the environmental driver, with breakpoints only permitted between adjacent time points; a regime shift was classified as a critical transition only when a sudden shift in plankton density was matched by an equivalent sudden shift in environmental state space in response to a small change in the abiotic driver, together with bimodality of plankton density over the whole series and evidence of hysteresis (overlap of TGAM smooths/clusters in state space). Series with a breakpoint but no matched state-space breakpoint were classified as "abrupt non-bifurcations" if bimodal; the two classes relevant to EWS evaluation are "critical transitions" vs "not critical transitions" (i.e., critically transitioning vs non-transitioning fate). The outcome is thus an ecosystem/trophic-level regime shift, not a population collapse threshold.

main_result: VERIFIED (abstract, multiple sources): The authors classified the temporal dynamics of surplus-production ("productivity") time series for 315 agency-assessed fish stocks worldwide and detected productivity abrupt shifts (PAS) in more than a quarter of stocks; abrupt declines were markedly overrepresented in marine regions with the highest warming rates, abrupt increases were more likely under lower fishing intensity, and "abrupt productivity declines preceded stock collapses by about a decade in a quarter of the stocks that shifted" (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42685203/; https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aed7911). VERIFIED (results-section snippets, PMC/science.org; single-snippet, medium confidence): PAS found in 25.7% of stocks (N = 81), with 13.3% negative (N = 42) and 12.4% positive (N = 39); other trajectory types (quadratic, linear, no change) found in similar proportions; regionally, NW Atlantic (30%) and NW Pacific (29%) had the highest share of negative PAS, SW Pacific the most positive PAS (32%) (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aed7911). VERIFIED (PMC snippet, single-source, medium confidence): among stocks that collapsed, the proportion with a negative PAS was 23% versus 12% among stocks that did not collapse; collapsed stocks on average experienced a stronger-magnitude negative PAS; "most of the negative PASs occurred between 4 and 12 years before the stock collapsed"; and "not all negative PASs led to stock collapse, with only 11 of 42 stocks (26%) having negative PAS followed by stock collapse" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13537261/). VERIFIED (press releases): a stock that experienced an abrupt productivity decline had "twice the risk of collapsing, on average 12 years later"; ocean-warming speed was the primary explanatory factor for abrupt declines (https://www.umontpellier.fr/articles/detecter-le-declin-des-stocks-de-poisson-permettrait-deviter-leffondrement-des-pecheries; https://toutmontpellier.fr/news/pecheries-des-chercheurs-montpellierains-identifient-un-signal-d-alert). This is the whole-series classification framework of Pélissié, Devictor & Dakos 2024 (Biological Conservation 290:110429), in which asdetect is used as the independent method and both methods must agree on the shift date within a 5-year tolerance (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000632072300530X; https://github.com/matpelissie/abrupt_shifts_ecological_timeseries_classification). Because the abrupt-change model is fitted to the full series (including post-shift and post-collapse data), shift dates are located with hindsight; the "precedes collapse by X years" statistic is a retrospective ordering of two dated events, not a forecast issued at a sequential origin. No search result mentioned forecast origins, rolling/expanding windows, hindcasts, or predictors computed only from data available up to a given year (queries with "hindcast", "out-of-sample", "real-time", "retrospectively" returned nothing paper-specific).
design_out_of_sample: None visible. No train/test split, cross-validation, hindcast, or held-out evaluation appears in any snippet; the only robustness elements visible are (i) an independent breakpoint method to validate abrupt classifications and (ii) alternative collapse thresholds (10% of max; 15%, 25%, 50% of average biomass) (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aed7911). Inference: the collapse–PAS association is an in-sample retrospective association across stocks, not an out-of-sample predictive evaluation.
design_baseline: No forecasting baseline visible. The comparison reported is between stock groups: proportion of negative PAS among collapsed (23%) vs non-collapsed (12%) stocks, and the magnitude of negative PAS in collapsed vs non-collapsed stocks (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13537261/). No comparator based on current abundance relative to a reference, recent biomass slope, B/BMSY status, or a state-space threshold-crossing forecast appears in any snippet; no comparison against a null/surrogate model or a conventional forecast is visible. The statistical test used for the association (e.g., logistic regression, Fisher/chi-square) is not visible in search results.
design_calibration: Not visible / apparently not applicable: no alarm thresholds, probability calibration, ROC/AUC, or threshold-matching are mentioned in any snippet. The "signal" is a categorical classification outcome (negative PAS yes/no) from AICc model selection, not a continuous score with a calibrated alarm threshold.
design_false_alarms: Partially addressed, descriptively. VERIFIED (PMC snippet): the paper explicitly reports that "not all negative PASs led to stock collapse, with only 11 of 42 stocks (26%) having negative PAS followed by stock collapse", and that negative PAS occurred in 12% of non-collapsed stocks vs 23% of collapsed stocks (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13537261/). So non-transitioning (non-collapsing) stocks are in the sample and shifted-but-uncollapsed stocks are counted; this is consistent with our stance that prior work did not ignore false positives. NOT VISIBLE: any explicit false-alarm rate/budget, any matching of alarm burden between methods, any treatment of negative PAS that occurred after a collapse (the 11/42 phrase says "followed by", so the ordering was checked, but how post-collapse or concurrent PAS were counted is not visible), and any exclusion window near series ends or handling of stocks whose PAS occurred too recently to have had time to collapse (i.e., right-censoring).
design_horizon_and_censoring: No fixed forecast horizon: lead time is a descriptive distribution of years between the dated PAS and the dated collapse ("most negative PASs occurred between 4 and 12 years before the stock collapsed", PMC snippet; "about a decade in a quarter of the stocks that shifted", abstract; "on average 12 years", press; preprint version "ten to twenty years in 25% of the cases") (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13537261/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42685203/; https://www.umontpellier.fr/articles/detecter-le-declin-des-stocks-de-poisson-permettrait-deviter-leffondrement-des-pecheries; https://ecoevorxiv.org/repository/view/9253/). Right-censoring: not visible in search results whether stocks with a recent negative PAS and short subsequent follow-up were treated as non-collapse (i.e., whether incomplete follow-up was counted as a negative outcome) — this is exactly the "complete follow-up" gap our design targets, but I cannot confirm from snippets that the paper mishandled it; treat as unknown.
what_it_does_NOT_do_relative_to_our_task: Relative to our planned design, the paper (based on what is visible) does NOT: (1) use classical critical-slowing-down EWS (trend in lag-1 autocorrelation and variance) as the predictor — its "warning signal" is an abrupt shift in surplus production identified by AICc model selection; a search pairing the title with "autocorrelation"/"variance"/"critical slowing down" returned only unrelated EWS papers; (2) perform sequential, fixed-horizon (1–5 y) prediction from time-indexed forecast origins — classification uses the whole series with hindsight; (3) evaluate anything out-of-sample or via hindcast; (4) compare against a state-and-trend or state-space threshold-crossing forecasting baseline; (5) calibrate any alarm threshold or match false-alarm burden across methods; (6) impose an explicit false-alarm budget (it reports 26% of negative-PAS stocks subsequently collapsed and 12% of non-collapsed stocks had negative PAS, but no operating-point analysis); (7) address right-censoring/complete follow-up (not visible either way); (8) extend beyond marine RAM Legacy stocks — no GPDD, LPD, BioTIME, FishGlob, or lakes; (9) group by biological system or use capacity-matched learners; (10) report a detection delay for the shift itself in real time (how many post-shift years are needed before the classifier flags a PAS) — not visible. Its outcome (biomass < 25% of to-date average) is a collapse threshold on abundance, which overlaps our outcome class, and its data source (RAM Legacy) overlaps one of our candidate datasets.
threat_reasoning: This is the nearest published neighbor to our study on data source (RAM Legacy), outcome (abundance-defined stock collapse), and framing (a signal that "precedes collapse by ~a decade", promoted in press as a warning system with a "12-year" lead), it is in a high-profile venue, it explicitly quantifies shifted-but-uncollapsed stocks (11/42 negative-PAS stocks collapsed; 12% of non-collapsed stocks had a negative PAS), and it was published one week before our Stage 0 date, so reviewers will expect us to position against it. However, on the methodological combination we claim as novel, the overlap is minimal: it is a retrospective, whole-series, in-sample association study with no sequential forecast origins, no out-of-sample evaluation, no forecasting baseline, no calibration, no false-alarm budget, and no explicit follow-up/censoring handling, and its predictor is a productivity regime-shift classification rather than an AR(1)/variance EWS score. Rated "moderate" rather than "low" because of the overlap in data, outcome and public framing; rated below "high" because none of the seven design elements in our novelty claim are present. Positioning suggestion for the manuscript: cite it as motivating evidence that a precursor exists in RAM Legacy, note that its 26% positive-predictive fraction is retrospective, and optionally add its collapse definition (<25% of to-date mean biomass) as a preregistered sensitivity outcome. main_result: Static (non-temporal) classification study. The authors (i) classified each fish time series into a shape class (no change / linear / quadratic / abrupt) by AICc model comparison with asdetect confirmation, (ii) computed a "dynamical footprint" of 7 stability metrics (DEV = dominant eigenvalue from S-map Jacobian, lag-1 AR, SD, CV, disparity, dispersion, skewness), each as a full-series value and as a Kendall-tau trend over a rolling window of 50% of series length, and (iii) trained a gradient-boosted tree model (caret::train, method xgbTree; snippet reports 100 rounds, max depth 3, learning rate 0.1, gamma 0) to predict abrupt vs nonabrupt from the footprint, one model per dataset ("context-specific"), evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation. Reported performance: on simulated series 96% accuracy (AUC ~1), dropping to 75% accuracy (AUC ~0.93) under high demographic noise; on empirical data "moderate" performance with LOO AUC = 0.84 (RAM Legacy productivity), 0.75 (ICES Atlantic cod CPUE), 0.65 (FishGlob CPUE); lowest sensitivity for the abrupt class was 40% in FishGlob (all from search snippets of the PNAS/PMC text: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2505461122 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12403094/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40825133/). Series that were shape-classified as nonabrupt but that the BRT predicted as abrupt were labelled "potential abrupt" and reported as 50 populations "at risk of future abrupt shifts" across 11 Large Marine Ecosystems (13 from RAM Legacy, 6 from ICES cod, 31 from FishGlob; examples named in snippets: black rockfish Sebastes melanops on the US West Coast, haddock M. aeglefinus in the North Atlantic, pink cusk-eel Genypterus blacodes). Confidence: high for the dataset/sample/AUC/BRT/LOO facts (each seen in at least two snippets or confirmed in the authors' code); medium for the 13/6/31 breakdown and the species examples (single snippet, though 13+6+31 = 50 is internally consistent).
what_it_does_NOT_do_relative_to_our_task: (1) No sequential/fixed-horizon prediction: each series receives one footprint and one predicted class; there are no forecast origins, no lead-time (1-5 yr) evaluation, and no statement of when a shift is expected (snippets and code; "timing" details not visible in search results). (2) Not a temporally out-of-sample design: validation is leave-one-out across series within each dataset, not across time; the footprint's rolling-window Kendall tau uses the whole available series (code: calc_roll_metrics). (3) Outcome is a retrospective trajectory-shape label ("abrupt" breakpoint model preferred by AICc and confirmed by asdetect), not a population collapse defined by an abundance threshold; whether abrupt shifts of both directions (increase and decrease) were pooled is not visible in search results. (4) No non-EWS comparator: no state/trend baseline, no null model, no conventional forecast; the only comparison is simulated vs empirical performance (the .Rhistory in the archive shows exploratory EWSNet/EWSmethods use, but nothing of that kind is visible in the published results). (5) No calibration step and no false-alarm budget: class = argmax of xgboost probabilities (code line 1070 of functions_dynclass.R); nonabrupt series predicted abrupt are reinterpreted as "potential abrupt"/at-risk rather than counted against an alarm budget. (6) No follow-up verification that the 50 flagged populations subsequently shifted; no censoring logic. (7) Fish stocks and survey CPUE only (RAM Legacy, ICES cod, FishGlob); no GPDD, Living Planet, BioTIME, lakes, or cross-realm grouping. (8) Only 629 of 9,006 series survived the >=20-year, no-missing-values filter; class counts within the 629 are not visible in search results. (9) Potential label-dependent windowing: the archived code's detandcut() truncates abrupt-class series at the retrospectively estimated breakpoint when detrend.type = "asclassif" and cut = TRUE (the default in run_dynfoot), so abrupt-series footprints may be computed on the pre-shift segment while nonabrupt series use their full length; whether the published analysis used cut = TRUE is not visible in search results (inferred from code defaults and the ecoFAST_plots example call using detrend.type = "asclassif").
threat_reasoning: This is the closest fish-stock precedent for "EWS-type metrics predict proneness to abrupt shifts" at scale and it uses two of our candidate datasets (RAM Legacy and FishGlob) plus lag-1 AR and variance-type metrics, so it must be cited and positioned explicitly; any claim that we are the first to apply AR1/variance-type indicators to RAM Legacy or FishGlob at scale would be false. However, it contains none of the design elements in our novelty claim: no sequential fixed-horizon prediction, no temporal out-of-sample validation, no matched state/trend baseline, no calibration, no explicit false-alarm budget, and no complete outcome follow-up (flagged "at risk" populations are not verified against later data). Its outcome is a retrospective shape class rather than a collapse, and its evaluation is cross-sectional LOO. It is best positioned as a static "susceptibility classification" whose prospective-risk interpretation our prequential design directly tests. Note for positioning: the paper does treat non-transitioning series (nonabrupt classes) as the negative class and reports class-wise sensitivity (e.g., 40% abrupt-class sensitivity in FishGlob), so consistent with our stated stance we should not claim it ignored false positives; rather it reinterpreted them as at-risk populations.
design_time_indexed: No. Predictors were computed once per series, not at successive forecast origins. Search snippet: "Metrics were derived both across the entire time series and as a temporal trend, which was quantified by calculating Kendall's tau for each metric using an overlapping rolling window (window size: 50% of the time series length)" (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2505461122). Code confirms: calc_metrics() computes full-series DEV/SD/CV/disparity/dispersion/skew/ar1 and calc_roll_metrics(x, winsize=50) computes the Kendall tau of each metric over all overlapping windows spanning the series (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alejvcano/dynfoot2025/main/dynfoot.zip, functions_dynclass.R lines 80-165 and 487-527). Important nuance from code: detandcut(data, dettype, cut=TRUE) applies class-specific detrending ("asclassif": two-mean step model for abrupt, quadratic/linear fits otherwise) and, if dettype=="asclassif" & cut==TRUE, keeps only x <= breakpoint for abrupt-class series ("truncates data for 'abrupt' classifications at the change point"); run_dynfoot() defaults to cut=TRUE, min.length=20. So abrupt-series footprints may be pre-shift-only, but the cut point is the retrospectively estimated breakpoint (label-informed) and nonabrupt series are not truncated to matched lengths. Whether the published run used cut=TRUE and "asclassif" is not visible in search results (the related ecoFAST_plots example uses detrend.type="asclassif", min.length=30: https://github.com/O-Celia/ecoFAST_plots). No sequential origins in any case. Confidence: high that there were no sequential origins; medium on the truncation detail.
design_out_of_sample: Leave-one-out cross-validation across series within each dataset: "The predictive power of the BRT models was tested using leave-one-out cross-validation. The three models exhibited moderate performance with AUC of 0.84, 0.75, and 0.65 for the RAM Legacy, the ICES cod, and the FishGlob datasets, respectively" (snippet from https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2505461122). Code confirms a LOO loop that trains caret::train(method="xgbTree", trControl=trainControl(method="none")) on n-1 series and predicts the held-out one (functions_dynclass.R run_ml_model, lines ~1011-1078 and a second version ~1193-1291 that also supports a random train/test split with trainsetsize). Separate model per dataset ("context-specific"). Simulated series (data/simu/all_simu_eig_r1.rds) were used to benchmark (96% accuracy, AUC ~1; 75%, AUC ~0.93 under high demographic noise). Not temporally out-of-sample; no holdout of later years; no cross-dataset transfer results visible in search results. Confidence: high.

design_false_alarms: Non-transitioning series (no change, linear, quadratic) form the "nonabrupt" negative class, so class-wise errors are reported (snippet: lowest abrupt-class sensitivity 40% in FishGlob; a confusion-matrix plot function with per-class sensitivities exists in code). However, nonabrupt series that the BRT predicts as abrupt are not treated as false alarms: they are relabelled "potential abrupt" — "cases initially classified as 'nonabrupt' but exhibiting a dynamical footprint that the BRT model recognizes as sharing characteristics with 'abrupt' shifts" — and reported as the 50 at-risk populations (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2505461122). No false-alarm budget, no alarm-rate equalization, no verification of these flags against later data visible. Exclusions: series with missing values or <20 years removed (629 of 9,006 retained). For the shape classification, code applies an edge_lim ("minimal breakpoint distance to start or end dates") so breakpoints too close to series ends are not accepted as abrupt (functions_trajclass.R, best_traj_aic), which is a classification-validity rule rather than an outcome-censoring rule for prediction. Confidence: high on the "potential abrupt" reinterpretation (two snippets + code); medium on exclusion details.
design_horizon_and_censoring: No forecast horizon: the model predicts a whole-series shape class, not an event within k years. The "risk of future abrupt shifts" for the 50 flagged populations is asserted from footprint similarity, with no follow-up window, no right-censoring treatment, and no later-outcome verification visible in search results. Minimum series length 20 years; FishGlob/ICES CPUE and RAM productivity are annual series (implied by "length below 20 years"; exact temporal resolution not stated in snippets). Confidence: medium-high.
outcome_definition: Retrospective trajectory-shape class of each series, following the Pélissié, Devictor & Dakos (2024, Biological Conservation) framework (same lab; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000632072300530X ; https://github.com/matpelissie/abrupt_shifts_ecological_timeseries_classification). main_result: VERIFIED from the authors' manuscript source (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boettiger-lab/mee_tipping_point_forecasting/main/manuscript/manuscript.Rmd): the paper is a SIMULATION-ONLY methods comparison of probabilistic (distributional) time-series forecasting for three classic critical-transition scenarios: (1) supercritical Hopf bifurcation in a stochastic Nicholson-Bailey host-parasitoid model with linearly increasing host carrying capacity K (K0=14, delta=0.08); (2) saddle-node (fold) bifurcation in May's consumer-resource model with linearly increasing grazing parameter h (h0=0.15, alpha=0.000375, sigma=0.02); (3) a purely stochastic (noise-driven) transition between alternative stable states in May's model with fixed h=0.26. Six forecasters are compared: MCMC parameter estimation GIVEN THE TRUE MODEL (greta/TensorFlow Probability; treated as an idealized upper bound), ARIMA (lower-bound statistical baseline), and four deep-learning models from the darts library (LSTM, GRU, Block RNN, Transformer), each trained to output Laplace-distribution parameters per step and each an ensemble of 5 seeds; plus an unweighted 'ml_ensemble' pooling all non-MCMC forecasts. Skill is scored with strictly proper scores (CRPS and log score, scoringRules) against n=100 replicate simulations of the true future process. Abstract result (verified verbatim in Rmd and in the BONs.bib abstract, https://github.com/PoisotLab/BiodiversityObservationNetworks.jl/blob/3e481794cef326298078046ffef4cd5dbddda254/docs/BONs.bib): deep-learning models performed comparably to the idealized MCMC model on the stochastic-transition case (where a transition is present in the training data) and generally in between MCMC and ARIMA on the Hopf and saddle-node cases. Results text: only the MCMC model anticipates the sharp saddle-node transition; Block RNN and Transformer 'resemble a naive prediction extrapolating the last observed state'; ARIMA and ML 'fail to predict the qualitative shift in dynamic behavior' in the bifurcation scenarios; near-term forecasts 'may be very accurate right up to the transition event before becoming widely wrong'; the ML ensemble often scores as well as the best single ML model; score distributions are bimodal in the saddle (by horizon) and stochastic (by replicate) cases. The authors explicitly frame the task as quantitative probabilistic forecasting of future states, 'a very different question using very different methods' from the early-warning-signal literature (Scheffer et al. 2009; Bury et al. 2021), which they characterize as only answering the categorical 'is a transition coming?' question.
what_it_does_NOT_do_relative_to_our_task: VERIFIED from manuscript text and code: (1) No empirical population data at all -- every series is simulated from the Nicholson-Bailey or May models; none of RAM Legacy, FishGlob/ICES, GPDD, LPD, BioTIME or lake data appear (repo file tree shows only simulated csv/parquet forecasts and scores). (2) No binary 'collapse'/'transition' event outcome and no detection/alarm metric: the target is the full distribution of future states, scored by CRPS/log score; hit rate, lead time, sensitivity, precision, AUC, or 'fraction of collapses detected' are not reported (a helper count_tipped(threshold=0.3) exists in darts/utils.py but its use in reported results is not visible in the manuscript). (3) No EWS score of any kind -- no lag-1 autocorrelation, variance, Kendall tau trend, or any 'classical EWS' predictor is computed or benchmarked; EWS are discussed only in Introduction/Discussion as a different problem. (4) No state-and-trend baseline, no threshold-crossing forecast, no state-space model, no capacity-matched learners; baselines are ARIMA and true-model MCMC. (5) No sequential/rolling forecast origins: each scenario uses a single fixed origin at the end of the training window (Hopf t=100, saddle t=250, stochastic t=0 with one prior transitioned replicate as training); the Discussion states 'our analysis has focused on the task of making a single forecast prior to the occurrence of a critical transition' and leaves iterative data assimilation to future work. (6) No false-alarm budget, no calibration analysis (reliability/coverage), no non-transitioning control series in the bifurcation scenarios (all 100 replicate futures undergo the bifurcation because the parameter drifts deterministically), and no right-censoring issue (futures are fully simulated). (7) No cross-realm or grouped-by-system evaluation; no fixed 1-5-year-ahead horizon in calendar units (time steps are model generations / dimensionless). (8) No claim about real-world lead-time skill; the authors state they cannot claim ML will translate to real data with missing/sparse/error-laden observations.
threat_reasoning: The paper addresses a different question (quantitative probabilistic state forecasting of simulated critical transitions with deep learning) rather than binary early detection of population collapse in empirical monitoring data. It contains none of the elements of our novelty claim: no empirical multi-realm abundance data, no EWS predictor, no state/trend or threshold-crossing baseline, no calibration to a shared false-alarm budget, no sequential fixed-horizon origins, no complete-follow-up outcome design. Its evaluation is a single-origin temporal hold-out on simulated replicates scored by proper scoring rules. It is best positioned in our manuscript as (a) a prior demonstration, from the Boettiger lab, that phenomenological forecasters (ARIMA, RNNs, Transformers) behave like naive last-state extrapolation and are accurate 'right up to the transition event' -- which directly motivates our inclusion of a state-and-trend baseline as the relevant comparator; (b) a precedent for strictly proper probabilistic scoring and for explicitly comparing against an idealized upper bound; and (c) a source of the open question they pose about whether training on 'analogous' systems (e.g., other lakes) can transfer, which our pooled, system-grouped hindcast partly addresses. It does not preempt the combination we claim. One caution for positioning: the paper explicitly distinguishes forecasting from EWS 'categorical' prediction, so we should not describe it as an EWS-evaluation study.

Everything below is extracted from the authors' public code repository (github.com/ThomasMBury/deep-early-warnings-pnas), whose README identifies it as the code 'to reproduce results in the publication'. What the repository shows the paper did: (1) Trained a deep-learning classifier (Keras Sequential: Conv1D 50 filters kernel 12 -> dropout 0.1 -> MaxPool -> LSTM 50 -> dropout -> LSTM 10 -> dropout -> Dense softmax over 4 classes: fold, Hopf, transcritical, null) on a synthetic library of residual time series generated from randomly parameterised 2-D polynomial (up to cubic) dynamical systems whose bifurcations were located with AUTO-07P, simulated stochastically up to the bifurcation with a change-point algorithm locating the transition, keeping ts_len points prior to transition; nulls are fixed-parameter runs. Library sizes stated in README: 500,000 series of length 500 (the '500-classifier') and 200,000 of length 1500 (the '1500-classifier'), 1000 per class per batch of 4000. 20 networks trained (10 with random left+right zero padding, 10 left-only); reported predictions are the mean over the 20. (2) Compared the DL 'probability of any bifurcation' (fold+Hopf+transcritical) against Kendall-tau trends of rolling variance and lag-1 autocorrelation using ROC curves/AUC (sklearn roc_curve). (3) Test systems: May's harvesting model (fold), consumer-resource model (Hopf and transcritical), SEIRx model (variables x and I) with 10 forced and 10 null simulations each; empirical: thermoacoustic (Rijke tube) rate-dependent transitions (19 experiments; nulls = 2 random segments from each of 10 quasi-static experiments), 8 paleoclimate records from Dakos et al. 2008 (7 used in the ROC; 10 AR(1) surrogate nulls per record), and Mediterranean sapropel anoxia records from Hennekam et al. 2020 (13 transition series x 2 proxies Mo and U; 1 AR(1) surrogate null each). (4) The 8-panel ROC figure ('Fig 2 of manuscript' per fig_roc_combined.py) covers May fold, CR Hopf, CR transcritical, SEIRx x, SEIRx I, anoxia, thermoacoustic, climate, for the 'late' window; an 'early'-window version is a supplementary figure. AUC values present in the repository's exported ROC result files (these may have been regenerated with the 2025 TF-2.15 re-run and were NOT verified against the published figure): thermoacoustic late: DL 0.999, variance 0.933, lag-1 AC 0.952; anoxia late: DL 0.991, var 0.899, AC 0.594; paleoclimate late: DL 0.710, var 0.588, AC 0.749; May fold 500-classifier late: DL 0.987, var 0.874, AC 0.721; CR Hopf 500 late: DL 0.998, var 0.846, AC 0.631; SEIRx I late: DL 0.544, var 0.586, AC 0.563; SEIRx x late: DL 1.0, var 0.940, AC 0.894. The ewstools README (PyPI/GitHub) summarises the paper as showing that 'deep learning has shown great potential for predicting bifurcations and their type'.
what_it_does_NOT_do_relative_to_our_task: (a) No population-abundance monitoring data at all: no RAM Legacy, GPDD, Living Planet, BioTIME, survey indices, or lake time series; ecological content is limited to simulated May harvesting, consumer-resource and SEIRx models; empirical tests are a laboratory combustion (thermoacoustic) system, paleoclimate proxy records and sediment geochemistry (Mo, U). (b) Outcome is 'approach to a bifurcation' (known a priori for each forced series) versus 'no bifurcation' (null), not a first population collapse defined from abundance. (c) Not a fixed-horizon forecast: evaluation windows are defined as fractions of the pre-transition record ([0.6,0.8] 'early', [0.8,1.0] 'late'), which requires knowing the transition time to place the window; there is no 1-5-year (or any absolute) lead-time framing, and absolute lead time differs across series. (d) Not prequential: detrending (Lowess/Gaussian) and rolling variance/AC are computed once on the whole pre-transition series and only then are classifiers/Kendall tau applied to growing segments, so the residual at time t uses later observations; series are retrospectively aligned to the known transition. (e) No state-or-trend comparator: the only baselines are variance and lag-1 AC Kendall tau; nothing like abundance relative to reference, recent slopes, or a state-space threshold-crossing forecast. (f) No threshold calibration to a common false-alarm budget: comparison is threshold-free AUC; the 'negatives' are fixed-parameter simulations, AR(1) surrogates fitted to the first 20% of residuals, or quasi-static experiments, not real non-collapsing populations from the same monitoring programme. (g) No probability calibration assessment visible. (h) No right-censoring problem exists because every series' outcome is known, so 'complete follow-up' is not addressed as a design issue. (i) No grouping by biological system and no capacity-matched learners (a 20-network CNN-LSTM ensemble is compared with a single summary statistic). (j) Small empirical samples (19, 7-8, 13x2 series). (k) The published text/abstract could not be inspected, so any additional analyses reported only in the paper or SI are not visible.
threat_reasoning: Bury et al. 2021 is a methods paper introducing a deep-learning classifier of bifurcation type trained on synthetic dynamical systems, evaluated by ROC/AUC on simulated models and three non-population empirical datasets with explicit null series. It overlaps with our task only in (i) using classical EWS (variance, lag-1 AC trends) as comparators and (ii) evaluating detection against non-transitioning negatives with ROC, which is why we must not claim prior work ignored false positives. It does not attempt population-collapse prediction in monitored ecological populations, fixed-horizon sequential forecasting, out-of-sample prequential origins, state/trend forecasting baselines, calibration to a false-alarm budget, or complete-follow-up handling; its windows are anchored on the known transition time, which is precisely the design feature our prequential hindcast departs from. It is therefore a key paper to cite and position against, not a threat to the stated combined novelty claim. Confidence in this judgement is limited by not having read the published text (see confidence field).
design_time_indexed: Partly. Predictors ARE computed at sequential origins: ewstools.apply_classifier_inc applies the classifier to segments from the series start up to tmax, incremented by 10 data points (the repo's dl_apply.py scripts use inc = 10*dt on the last 1500 or 500 residual points before the transition), left-zero-padding shorter segments and normalising by the mean absolute value; Kendall tau is likewise computed on the EWS series 'up to point t_fin' at regular spacings (compute_ktau.py). However, the residuals and rolling variance/AC fed into these are produced once on the full pre-transition series (ts.detrend + compute_var/compute_auto on the entire series in compute_ews.py / sim_*.py), so smoothing at time t uses data after t, and the evaluation windows are placed as fractions of the interval from series start to the known transition time. Evaluation takes 10 evenly spaced prediction times inside the window per series (forced and null) and pools them into one ROC. So: sequential origins yes; strictly causal/prequential no; window placement uses knowledge of the transition time.
design_out_of_sample: The DL classifier is trained on a synthetic library from random 2-D polynomial models with a train/validation/test split (groups.csv dataset_ID 1/2/3; ModelCheckpoint on val_accuracy; DL_training.py prints test accuracy/F1/confusion matrix on the synthetic test set) and is then applied to different mechanistic models (May, consumer-resource, SEIRx) and to empirical datasets never used in training, i.e. out-of-sample with respect to the training library. The classical EWS have no fitted parameters. There is no forward-in-time hold-out within a dataset, and ROC thresholds are swept on the evaluation data itself rather than selected on a held-out set.
design_baseline: Comparators are the classical EWS only: Kendall tau of rolling variance and of rolling lag-1 autocorrelation (rolling window 0.25 of series for models, 0.5 for empirical), computed after Lowess (span 0.2) or Gaussian-kernel detrending (bandwidths from Dakos 2008 Table S3 for paleoclimate; 0.2 or 0.09 for anoxia). The DL model's own 'null' class probability is recorded but the ROC indicator is the summed bifurcation probability. No current-state, trend/slope, null-model, or conventional forecast comparator is present in the repository.
design_false_alarms: Non-transitioning series are explicitly included as negatives (truth value 0): (i) models: 10 null simulations per model with the bifurcation parameter held fixed at its initial value (e.g. sim_may_fold_null.py bl=bh=0.15), evaluated in the same time window as the matching forced run; (ii) thermoacoustic: 2 randomly positioned 1500-point segments from each of 10 quasi-static (fixed-voltage) experiments (IDs 1-10 only, 'since the rest are already at the limit cycle') = 20 nulls vs 19 forced; (iii) paleoclimate: 10 AR(1) surrogates per record, with alpha and sigma fitted to the variance and lag-1 AC of the first 20% of that record's residuals, seed 0; (iv) anoxia: 1 AR(1) surrogate per series and proxy, same fitting rule. For each forced or null series, 10 evenly spaced predictions in the prediction window are taken 'so some transitions don't input more data to the ROC than others'; NaN Kendall taus are dropped (anoxia). Performance is summarised by threshold-free ROC/AUC; there is no fixed false-alarm budget, no threshold chosen, and no exclusion of origins near series ends (the 'late' window runs up to the transition point itself).
design_horizon_and_censoring: No fixed forecast horizon. Predictions are evaluated in relative windows: 'late' = [0.8,1.0] and 'early' = [0.6,0.8] of the interval from series start to the transition (models, thermoacoustic, paleoclimate); the anoxia script docstring describes these as roughly 0-1.5 kyr and 1.5-3 kyr before the transition. Training series are the ts_len (500 or 1500) points immediately prior to a change-point-detected transition. Because every forced series is known to end in a transition and every null is known not to, there is no censoring problem and no treatment of right-censored origins; 'complete follow-up' is not a design consideration in this paper.
design_calibration: Not visible in the repository. DL outputs are softmax class probabilities averaged over 20 networks; the only reported performance measures in the code are ROC/AUC on test systems and accuracy/F1/precision/recall/confusion matrix on the synthetic test set. No reliability diagram, Brier score, or threshold calibration step was found. Whether the published SI contains calibration analysis is not visible in search results.

threat_reasoning: Ward et al. 2014 is a forecast-accuracy meta-analysis, not an EWS or collapse-detection study: it has no event outcome, no alarms, no false-alarm budget, no calibration, and a single hold-out origin per series. It therefore does not pre-empt the combination we claim (sequential fixed-horizon origins + out-of-sample validation + matched state/trend baselines + calibration + false-alarm budget + complete follow-up for population collapse across realms). Its relevance is as a precedent and justification rather than a competitor: (a) it establishes, on 2379 vertebrate series including RAM Legacy productivity and LPI birds/mammals, that a last-observation (random-walk-without-drift) forecast is essentially unbeatable for non-cyclic species over 1-5-year horizons, which directly motivates and legitimises our 'current state' baseline and our capacity-matching concern ('estimation of even one or two parameters imposes a high cost'); (b) it uses scale-free hold-out error (MASE) and a held-out final-5-year window, an out-of-sample convention we extend to sequential origins; (c) it must be cited carefully because it did use lag-1 autocorrelation, variance of differences, depletion (current abundance relative to maximum) and trend as covariates of forecast error - superficially overlapping with our EWS and state features - but only as explanatory covariates of forecast accuracy in birds/fish, never as predictors of collapse. Citing papers on GitHub summarise it the same way (DanOvando/salmon-forecast-paper: 'They however found that the sorts of tools explored here generally performed worse than simple autoregressive models'; 'a lag(1) model, a conventional benchmark model for timeseries modeling [hyndman2006; ward2014]'). A residual risk to note in the manuscript: its finding that higher autocorrelation and lower variance correlate with better forecastability could be raised by reviewers as evidence that AR1/variance carry information about predictability, so we should position our EWS-vs-baseline test as distinct from forecast-accuracy covariates.
design_time_indexed: Partially, and only in the weakest sense (verified from Methods, 'Model fitting and projection', p. 655 of the PDF): 'The models were fit to the entire time series minus the last five time steps; this is the "training" data. The last five time steps were held out to gauge predictive performance ... From the fitted models, we forecasted the next 1 to 5 years using the prediction functions supplied with the corresponding R packages.' So predictors/parameters are computed only from data before the single forecast origin, but there is exactly ONE origin per series (fixed at n-5), not sequential origins; no rolling or expanding window evaluation. The RREEBES reproduction confirms: 'forecasts based on the training data (all data points except the five last data points)' and ASE computed for t = 1..5 after training (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/opetchey/RREEBES/gh-pages/WARD_etal_2014_Oikos/report/Ward_2014_report.html). Model hyper-parameters (GAM smoothness, local-regression neighbours/polynomial, Simplex embedding dimension) were chosen by cross-validation within the training data.
design_out_of_sample: Yes: a single hold-out of the final five observations per series; forecast error (absolute scaled error, ASE) computed for each of the 1-5 step-ahead predictions against the held-out observed values, then averaged across series to MASE (Hyndman & Koehler 2006). Stationary ARIMA models were fit to detrended training data with the trend included in the forecast. No cross-series or cross-origin cross-validation; no separate test set of series. Some model fits fail on some series (the reproduction reports MARSS failures on 5 series that were excluded; the paper itself does not report failure counts in the extracted text).
design_baseline: Yes - and this is the paper's central design element: 'The baseline model used in our analysis was a simple random walk without drift. For this model, the t-step ahead forecast is simply the last observed value' (p. 658-659); results are compared to 'RW-MASE' (MASE of that model, dashed lines in Figs 1-2). Additional comparators: random walk with drift (trend), state-space random walks with/without drift (StructTS, MARSS), ARIMA(p,d,q) with p,d,q in 0..2, exponential smoothing, structural time series, GAM on time, linear regression on time, local/kernel regression, neural nets (tsDyn nnetTs, m=1:3, d=1:2), Gaussian process (kernlab), random forest (lags 1-10, 500 trees), Simplex and S-MAP (Thorson code) - 49 models in total (Appendix Tables A1-A2). In our terminology their baseline corresponds to a 'current state' forecast; the RW-with-drift and state-space RW correspond to 'recent slope' / local-level state-space forecasts, but none is used to forecast a threshold crossing. There is no EWS model at all.
design_calibration: None. Only point forecasts are evaluated (ASE/MASE); no predictive intervals, probabilities, reliability diagrams or threshold calibration are reported in the extracted text. The ASE denominator uses the mean absolute one-step change within the training data (a total-variance scaling), which the authors note makes RW MASE exceed 1 for short series.
design_false_alarms: Not applicable / none: there are no alarms, events, classifications or positive/negative series. All 2379 series (whatever their trajectory) contribute forecast errors; no series are labelled as transitioning or non-transitioning. No exclusion near series ends beyond the design itself (the last five observations of every series are the test set, so every series contributes exactly 5 horizon-specific errors). Inclusion criteria: at least 25 continuous observations with no missing values, from a consistent survey; RAM Legacy SSB series excluded (smoothed assessment output), productivity (recruits/SSB) retained.
design_horizon_and_censoring: Horizons: 1 to 5 steps (years) ahead from the single origin at n-5 ('we forecasted the next 1 to 5 years'); Figs 1-2 display steps 1-4, Appendix Table A2 gives 1-step MASE for all 49 models, and the covariate analysis averages ASE over steps 1-3. Censoring: not an issue by construction - outcomes (observed values) exist for all five horizons in every series because the test window is the observed tail; no right-censored origins, no lead-time accounting, no event times.
